Hi Elena — thanks for the clear ask.

High level response:
- We can increase your reserved pool by +6 GPUs (from 8 -> 14) by Aug 1 and guarantee throughput targets tied to that reserved pool.
- For overflow we provide two supported modes:
  1) Soft overflow (recommended): automatic spillover onto on-demand capacity. Billed as usage (tokens / GPU-hour) at the overflow rate. Minimal latency uplift in normal conditions; worst-case added queueing during very large bursts.
  2) Hard cap: once reserved capacity is exhausted, requests are either queued with indefinite backpressure or returned with 429s/errors. This gives predictability on billing but increases application error handling responsibility.

Elena / team — quick technical breakdown to help with the latency/error estimates you requested. (I'm leaving this conversational so procurement/legal can digest.)

Short version: both modes are viable; tradeoffs below.

Soft-overflow (recommended for product continuity):
- Behavior: incoming requests beyond reserved capacity are routed to a burst pool (on-demand instances). We maintain the same runtime; KV cache misses and cold-starts can add latency.
- Expected performance:
  - +25% load: p95 increase ~10-18% depending on model sequence length (typical added latency 40-120ms).
  - +75% load: p95 increase ~30-60% and occasional p99 spikes during heavy churn.
- Operational note: we can configure a sliding surge band: first +2 GPUs at normal overflow rate, next +4 GPUs at +25% surcharge.

Hard cap (procurement-backstop):
- Behavior: after reserved capacity exhausted, requests are queued for up to 30s then rejected (429s).
- Expected performance:
  - Under the cap, p95 and error rates unchanged.
  - If traffic exceeds cap, error rate spikes quickly; client-side retries will compound load.
- Operational note: recommend adding a retry-backoff guideline and client-side queue strategy if you choose this path.

Attached: throughput_guarantee_table.csv — pragmatic numbers for expected tokens/sec per GPU and latency bands across sequence lengths.

If helpful, we can run a short load-run sim against your production traffic sample to produce precise numbers. That would take ~48 hours and a test key.
